description: Somos un equipo de amigos con perfil de ingeniería y apasionados por la tecnología. En este NASA Space Apps nos enfocado en el reto Dancing with the SARs, combinando Inteligencia Artificial, visión por computador y procesamiento de datos satelitales de radar para la detección de cambios ambientales. ¡Tenemos los roles cubiertos y estamos listos para darlo todo durante las 48 horas del hackathon!
summary:
The Friant-Kern Canal carries water by gravity to more than a million acres of farmland in California's San Joaquin Valley. When the ground under it sinks unevenly the canal loses slope and can carry less water. In its worst reach the canal has lost about 60% of its capacity, and repairing 33 miles of it costs around $500 million. STRAIN//CHAIN uses radar satellite data to find where this is happening and what it could mean for the canal.

We split 48 km of the canal into 25 stretches of 2 km each and measured ground motion along them with NASA OPERA DISP-S1 (Sentinel-1, ascending and descending orbits). Each stretch is compared with its neighbours. What bends the canal is a stretch that sinks more than the ones around it, so that difference is what we track. On 14 February 2026, 10 of the 25 stretches were sinking more than their neighbours. To check the method we compared it with independent InSAR points from California DWR. The differences agree with r = 0.995 (n = 7) (exploratory; the agreement still holds without the strongest point, r = 0.984). NISAR, GRACE, HLS and a few other NASA layers are shown as context. 

On top of this, a hydraulic engine written in C++ lets anyone ask "what if this stretch sank another 200 mm?" and see how much margin and capacity the canal would lose. Every figure on the site cites its source. One page lists what we don't claim.
details:
STRAIN//CHAIN is a web platform about land subsidence under the Friant-Kern Canal. The Panel shows the 25 stretches of the 48 km we studied, both on a map and on a timeline of satellite passes since 2024. For each stretch it shows the ground velocity, the difference with its neighbours over 1 km, the date it was first detected and what is nearby (roads, crossings and other assets taken from OpenStreetMap). On the Simulation page you choose a stretch, a canal cross-section and an extra amount of sinking. A hydraulic engine then calculates how much freeboard and carrying capacity would remain. "How we know" explains each data source, the method, the cross-check against an independent source and the limits of the analysis. "In short" is a one-minute guided tour for non-specialists.

The Explore menu has four more pieces made by the team. Truth Lens shows how a radar signal can fool you and how to detect it by comparing two sources. The Canal's Memory tells the story of the canal in five short acts (about 90 seconds). In the Subsidence Game you manage a canal over three turns, check the sources and then review your decisions. Vision 4D is a 3D tour of the canal where you move through time from 2018 to 2026, and it always marks what is measured data and what is only illustration. The site is available in English and Spanish.

How it works

1. Measure. OPERA DISP-S1 gives ground motion along the satellite line of sight. Combining an ascending and a descending Sentinel-1 orbit we get vertical motion next to the canal axis.

2. Compare stretches. A smoothed profile along the axis gives the slope and the curvature of each 2 km stretch. A stretch is flagged when its signal beats the noise, using a threshold corrected for multiple comparisons (Šidák). We do not flag a stretch just because the whole valley is sinking.

3. Cross-check. We compared OPERA with the California DWR / TRE Altamira InSAR points, which are processed independently. Comparing differences between points, both sources agree (r = 0.995, MAE 6.13 mm/yr, n = 7). Comparing absolute values is fragile: r drops from 0.943 to 0.565 if one point (fkc_11_R, which sinks about 60 mm per year) is removed. We show both results.

4. Context. A SQLite database built by the team holds 148,144 catalogued scenes and 1,151,606 observations from 27 sources (NISAR GCOV and GUNW, GRACE/GRACE-FO, HLS, ECOSTRESS, GPM IMERG, NASA POWER, SMAP, NASADEM, OPERA DSWx, DIST and RTC, and others). They help explain the why: the regional groundwater low in GRACE at the end of 2022 matches the year with the most sinking. None of them is used as an input to the simulation.

5. Simulate. A hydraulic engine written in C++ computes the water profile of a stretch under a subsidence you choose (a bowl shape, 0 to 1,000 mm). It returns the margin to the canal edge and the largest flow that keeps that margin. The cross-sections are a typical USBR shape and a test canal, so the result is a hypothetical exercise and not today's real capacity.

6. NISAR. We processed a provisional NISAR GUNW interferogram over the canal (track 114, descending, 8–20 October 2026): a profile of 489 stations every 500 m, 87% valid, with 40 random pixels checked against the original HDF5 file. Along the way we found that the product's "correction applied" flags refer to geolocation, not to the phase: the unwrapped phase still contained the ionospheric screen (correlation 0.95), and removing it cut the phase scatter from 5.5 to 1.7 rad. Because the product is provisional and covers a single 12-day pair, we show it as context, not as evidence of subsidence.

Benefits and impact

Canal operators and water districts spend a lot on surveys and repairs. A map that says "these stretches are bending, start here" can help decide where to look first. It also gives farmers and the public a way to see the problem with data they can check: every number has its source, unit, date and maturity (observed, processed, provisional or synthetic), and the data can be downloaded as JSON and CSV.

Tools

Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, Plotly, TanStack Query, Zod. Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLite, and a C++ hydraulic solver built with CMake. Data access through NASA Earthdata, ASF DAAC and PO.DAAC. Tests with Vitest, Playwright and pytest (more than 1,000 automated tests across the project).

What we considered

Radar measures along the line of sight, not vertically, so we only use vertical values where both orbits allow it. Velocities are relative to an OPERA reference point because there is no GNSS tie. NISAR products are still provisional, so they are context and not evidence. There is no forecast: no predictive model we tried beat "it will stay the same". A "detected" stretch is a statistical class, not a damage threshold. The canal axis comes from OSM/NHD 2010 and was not surveyed on site.

Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, to help write and review code, tests and documentation, and to draft and translate the website texts. About 7 in 10 commits in our repository list it as co-author. AI tools also helped with parts of the presentation, the demo video and the visual design. The team chose the method and checked the results against independent sources.

Team

Bernini (main web, Data Hub, NASA database), Daniel (NISAR processing chain, radar-hydraulics scenarios), Samuel (hydrology DWR-OPERA, live data mode, Vision 4D), Dairon (canal physics, per-stretch OPERA analysis, The Canal's Memory, Vision 4D radar tour), Pencho (C++ hydraulic engine, Subsidence Game) and Denis (per-stretch NASA layers and exposure, Truth Lens, web redesign).
